title: Double Life Drama
description: You're a regular student at Westwood Academy — except you're secretly Nova, a rising pop star with a growing fanbase. Nobody at school knows. Until now.
artStyle: bright pop-art illustration, glossy fashion magazine aesthetic, bold pinks and purples, Y2K meets modern teen drama style
mood: dramatic, glittery and full of heart

nodes.title: First Day Back at Westwood
nodes.prose:
Your name is {PLAYER_NAME}, and you have a secret.

You are also Nova — a pop star with 200,000 followers, a growing Spotify presence, and a debut single that music blogs are calling "the sound of the summer." Nobody at Westwood Academy knows. Not your teachers. Not the girls in Year 8. Nobody.

Today is the first day back. Your backpack has a hidden pocket with a sparkly phone case you only use for Nova business. Your regular phone case is plain grey. This is called professionalism.

In the cafeteria, two things happen at once. At the most sought-after table in school, Madison Clarke — glossy, terrifying, the girl who once made a teacher cry just by raising an eyebrow — is handing out gold-envelope party invitations. Not everyone gets one.

At a table by the window, a girl you've never seen is sitting alone, drawing something in a notebook. She's wearing a t-shirt that says the name of your favourite artist. She looks like she might be the most interesting person in this school.

You have about thirty seconds before the moment passes.

choices.text: Walk over to Madison's table — getting that invitation matters

choices.text: Sit with the new girl — that t-shirt is a sign

nodes.title: The Inner Circle Test
nodes.prose:
Madison's table smells like expensive perfume and danger.

There are five girls. They all look at you like you're a maths problem they haven't decided whether to solve. Madison herself is wearing sunglasses indoors. She does not remove them.

"{PLAYER_NAME}," she says, as if she's read your file. "We have a tradition. Anyone who wants an invitation to my party has to complete a tiny little task. It's not a big deal. It's just... a test of loyalty."

She slides her phone across the table. On the screen is a photo of Lily Chen — your old best friend before you drifted apart last year — at a dance recital. She's mid-jump and it's not her best angle.

"Post this to the Year 8 group chat with a caption. Something funny." Madison smiles. It doesn't reach her eyes. "Show me you're serious about being here."

The phone sits between you. At the other side of the cafeteria, you can see the new girl still drawing, unbothered by any of this.

nodes.title: Zara's Secret
nodes.prose:
Her name is Zara. She transferred from a performing arts school in London. She's drawing a stage layout in her notebook.

"Cool shirt," you say, sitting down. She looks up and grins — a real grin, not a calculated one.

"Thanks. I've been to three of her gigs." She tilts her head. "You look familiar. Like, really familiar."

Your stomach drops.

"I just have one of those faces," you say.

She pulls out her phone and shows you a saved Instagram post. It's Nova — you, in full stage makeup and a silver jacket — performing at a festival last summer. "You have the same eyes," says Zara simply. "And the same nervous thing you're doing with your hands right now."

You go very still.

"I'm not going to tell anyone," she says quickly. "I actually think what you're doing is incredible. I'm a songwriter. I've been working on something that would be perfect for Nova's next single." She pauses. "I just need the right voice."

The cafeteria buzzes around you. Madison is still handing out gold envelopes. Neither of you notices.

nodes.title: Viral for the Wrong Reasons
nodes.prose:
You posted it. The caption was mildly mean. Fourteen people laughed-reacted within sixty seconds.

Madison handed you a gold envelope with a satisfied smile. "I knew you had it in you."

By lunch, Lily Chen had seen it. You watched her read it from across the corridor. Her face did something complicated and then went very still. She put her phone away and walked in the opposite direction.

By 3pm, the post had 47 comments. Some were funny. Some were not. Lily hadn't replied to any of them.

That night, you sat in your bedroom with your Nova phone in one hand and your regular phone in the other. Your Nova DMs were full of fans asking about your next release. Your regular messages had one unread: from Lily. It just said: "Wow."

You have the golden envelope on your desk. The party is Saturday. Madison texted to say you're officially "in."

You're in. Is this what in feels like?

choices.text: Stay loyal to Madison — you're in the circle now, don't blow it

choices.consequence: Madison will not forgive this. But Lily might.

nodes.title: Standing Your Ground
nodes.prose:
You pushed the phone back.

"No thanks," you said. Quietly. Clearly.

Madison removed her sunglasses for the first time. The table went silent. "Excuse me?"

"I'm not posting that. It's mean and Lily's done nothing to anyone."

You picked up your bag and walked away. Behind you, you heard one of Madison's group whisper something. You didn't look back.

By the end of the day, you were officially off the party list. Three girls who'd smiled at you that morning blanked you in the corridor. A boy in your form gave you a small nod of respect, which helped slightly.

That evening, still buzzing with leftover adrenaline, you opened your Nova account. The school talent show had just been announced — with a record label talent scout in attendance. The prize: a studio session and industry mentoring.

You stared at the announcement for a long time. You had two options forming in your mind, each one terrifying in a different way.

nodes.title: Writing the Song
nodes.prose:
Zara's melody was, genuinely, the best thing you'd heard in months.

She'd written it on her phone's voice memo app in the back of a geography lesson. It was raw and funny and real — a song about pretending to be fine when everything is chaos. You added a hook in twenty minutes flat. The two of you stared at what you'd just created.

"That's a hit," you said.

"That's definitely a hit," she agreed.

You spent the next three weeks finishing it. You'd meet in the music room at lunch, swapping lyrics on your phones, laughing too loudly for the library. Zara was the first person at this school who knew who you actually were — all of you — and somehow that made the music better.

The school talent show announcement changed everything. A real talent scout. A real prize. Zara grabbed your arm in the corridor. "We have to do this. You have to do this."

You looked at the poster. Your name — your real name — wasn't known. Nova's name was. If you performed, people would find out.

nodes.title: The Secret Gets Out
nodes.prose:
"I don't know what you're talking about," you said.

Zara's smile faded. She looked at the photo, then at you, then back at the photo. "The eyes are literally identical. And you're doing the hand thing again."

"Lots of people have brown eyes and nervous hands," you said.

She nodded slowly, but she didn't look convinced. She put her phone away. "Okay. Sorry. My mistake."

It should have felt like relief. It didn't.

Two days later, Madison — who had apparently been listening from the next table the whole time — cornered you near the lockers. "So," she said, in a voice like a key turning in a lock. "You're Nova."

Your whole body went cold.

"I heard everything. Zara's not great at whispering." Madison tilted her head. "Now here's the thing. I could tell everyone — and you'd be the most famous person in school — or you could make it worth my while to stay quiet. Your choice."

You had about ten seconds to decide.

nodes.title: Making It Right
nodes.prose:
You deleted the post at 11:43pm.

You typed the apology for forty minutes. You deleted it six times. The final version was honest and didn't make excuses, which was harder to write than you expected.

You posted it to the group chat and then put your phone face-down on your pillow and stared at the ceiling.

Madison texted: "You are SO off the list." Three fire emojis.

Lily texted, twenty minutes later: "Thank you. That took guts." One small star emoji.

You slept better than you had in weeks.

The next day at school, Lily sat with you at lunch. She didn't bring up the post. You didn't either. You talked about music instead — she'd been listening to Nova's single on repeat. "Whoever Nova is, she gets it," said Lily.

You smiled and said nothing.

The talent show poster was on every noticeboard. Record label scout. Studio session prize. A week away. You had a decision to make — and this time it felt less like a trap and more like an open door.

nodes.title: Queen Bee, No Honey
nodes.prose:
The party was enormous. Madison's house had a DJ, a photo booth, and a hot chocolate bar. Everyone kept telling you how glad they were you were there.

You posted seven stories. You danced for two hours. You wore the gold envelope in your jacket pocket like a badge.

Lily was absent for three days after the post. When she came back, she sat somewhere new. She didn't look at you.

The talent show happened. You didn't enter — too risky, too much exposure. The talent scout came and went. A girl from Year 9 with an acoustic guitar got the studio session.

Madison threw another party the following month. You were on the list, but something felt different. The conversations were the same. The sunglasses were the same. And somewhere on your Nova account, your followers were asking why you hadn't posted new music in weeks.

You looked at Madison across the room and realised you'd traded the wrong things for the wrong things.

The crown didn't fit. It never does when you stole it.

nodes.title: The Kindness Goes Viral
nodes.prose:
Nova's post went up at 9pm. No explanation, no caption — just a voice memo you recorded in your bedroom of a song called "Sit With Her."

By midnight it had 12,000 streams. By morning, 40,000. Someone at Westwood posted it to the school group chat. By lunchtime, everyone was listening to it in the corridor on their phones.

Nobody knew Nova was at their school. The mystery made it bigger.

Madison heard it in the cafeteria and went quiet for a long time. You watched her face and didn't say anything.

The talent show came. You performed as Nova — masked, silver jacket, no name given. The talent scout sat in the front row. You sang "Sit With Her" live for the first time.

The scout offered you a development call the next morning. "I don't know who you are," she said, "but I want to."

You smiled. You'd decide when to tell her. On your own terms, in your own time.

The secret was yours. So was the music. So was everything.

nodes.title: Just You
nodes.prose:
You signed up for the talent show as {PLAYER_NAME}. No alias. No costume. No safety net.

Madison laughed when she saw the list. One of her friends sent you a voice note saying it was brave. The word brave landed funny — like it was a compliment and a warning at the same time.

The night of the show, you stood backstage in your regular clothes. Your hands were shaking. You had sung in front of 2,000 people as Nova at a festival. You had never sung as yourself, in front of 200 people who knew your name.

Madison was in the audience. The talent scout was in the third row.

You walked out. You sat down at the piano. You played the song you'd written last summer — the one that became Nova's first single — but you played it slowly, stripped back, just voice and keys.

Somewhere in the second chorus, Madison stopped whispering.

By the last note, the room was completely still.

Then it wasn't.

nodes.title: Nova Takes the Stage
nodes.prose:
You and Zara had rehearsed the reveal eighteen times. You had a plan for every version of how it could go wrong.

None of that prepared you for actually doing it.

You walked out as Nova — silver jacket, full hair, the stage makeup Zara had done in the school toilets with a surprisingly steady hand. The audience buzzed, confused.

You sang the first verse. You and Zara's harmonies locked perfectly. The chorus hit and the room lifted.

And then, at the bridge, you reached up and took off the wig.

For about two seconds, nobody breathed.

Then someone screamed. Then everyone was screaming. Somewhere in the audience, Madison Clarke's mouth was open and she had completely forgotten to look unbothered.

The talent scout was on her feet.

Zara grabbed your hand as the last note faded. You both stood in the spotlight — {PLAYER_NAME} and Zara, and also Nova — and the line between those things didn't feel like a secret anymore. It felt like a beginning.

nodes.title: Zara's Moment
nodes.prose:
She walked out onto that stage and owned every centimetre of it.

Zara performed your song — the one you wrote together — solo, acoustic, voice completely unprocessed. She'd told the audience she'd co-written it with "someone who wanted to stay behind the scenes for now." A spotlight hit the empty chair beside her.

The talent scout was very still for the entire performance.

Afterwards, backstage, Zara was shaking. The scout had asked to speak with her. She grabbed your arm. "Come with me."

You shook your head. "This one's yours."

She stared at you for a moment, then hugged you so hard your feet left the floor.

The scout signed Zara to a development deal. The co-writing credit was already on the contract — your name, your real name, as songwriter.

You walked home that night with nothing to show for it except the knowledge that you'd made something real with someone real, and that it had reached people, and that was more than enough.

For tonight.

nodes.title: Full Confession
nodes.prose:
You posted it on the school's Instagram page at 8am before anyone arrived.

A video. You in your bedroom, no makeup, no wig, phone propped on a stack of books. "Hi. My name is {PLAYER_NAME}. I'm in Year 8 at Westwood Academy. I'm also Nova. I've been keeping that a secret for two years and I'm done."

You talked for four minutes. About why you kept it hidden. About how weird and lonely it sometimes was. About how someone tried to use it against you and that made you realise the only person who should get to tell your story was you.

By the time you walked into school, 3,000 people had watched it.

Madison was in the corridor. She opened her mouth. You walked straight past her.

Zara was waiting at your locker. She didn't say anything. She just handed you a coffee and fell into step beside you.

The talent scout emailed that afternoon. "Saw the video. The authenticity is exactly what we look for. Let's talk."

You had been so afraid of this moment for so long. Turns out the thing you were afraid of was also the door.

nodes.title: The Mess You Made
nodes.prose:
You told Madison it was Zara who was making things up.

Madison believed you — or pretended to — and told half the school that the new girl was obsessed with Nova and was claiming to know her. By Tuesday, Zara was getting weird looks in the corridor.

She found you on Wednesday. She wasn't angry. She was just quiet, which was worse. "I thought we were going to be friends," she said. She didn't wait for an answer.

Madison, meanwhile, hadn't actually kept your secret — she'd just been biding her time. On Friday she posted a poll to the year group: "Is {PLAYER_NAME} actually Nova? Vote below." 74% said yes.

You denied it. Nobody believed you. Zara had already moved tables. Lily was still not talking to you. Madison found the whole thing deeply entertaining.

You had lost the friendship before it started, protected a secret nobody believed anymore, and made a mess of everything in the process.

Sometimes you make the wrong call. The good news: it's Year 8. You have time to do better.

nodes.title: Nova at Westwood
nodes.prose:
You walked onto the stage in the silver jacket and the full hair and the stage makeup that Lily had — once she'd stopped being speechless — actually helped you put on.

She found out ten minutes before you went on. You showed her the Nova account, the followers, the festival footage. She sat on the toilet lid in the school bathroom and stared at her phone for a full minute.

"This is INSANE," she said.

"I know."

"I've been listening to your MUSIC."

"I know."

"We're having a very long conversation after this."

"Deal."

You performed three songs. On the third one, the wig came off. The audience lost their minds. Madison, in the front row, looked like someone had gently removed the floor from beneath her feet.

The talent scout was already calling her office before the applause finished.

Lily was side-stage losing her voice screaming for you. That part — that exact part — was the best moment of the whole night.

nodes.title: Better Than Famous
nodes.prose:
"You want to perform together?" Lily stared at you. "I haven't performed anything since Year 6."

"Perfect. Same."

"I play piano badly."

"I'll sing. You play badly. It'll be charming."

She laughed. It sounded like something relaxing back into place.

You rehearsed in her bedroom for a week. You chose a song you'd both loved in primary school. You didn't tell her about Nova. Not yet. That conversation needed more time and better biscuits.

The talent show came. You were fourth on the bill, between a magic act and a surprisingly emotional recorder solo. You and Lily walked out, squinted at the lights, and Lily played three wrong notes in the intro and you both got the giggles and had to restart.

The audience laughed with you. Then you sang — really sang — and they went quiet.

You didn't win. The Year 9 with the acoustic guitar got the studio session.

But walking home with Lily afterwards, talking and laughing until your face hurt, you thought: the music would still be there tomorrow. This — right now — was harder to come by.
